episodes.167688: Ample instability and low-level vertical wind shear across central Indiana combined with a warm frontal boundary approaching from the south to produce several rotating, supercell thunderstorms.  These storms produced large hail within a two hour late day period over several of the region's southwestern to south-central counties||Soon after, a rotating cluster of thunderstorms crossed southern central Indiana during the evening and early morning hours.  This relative small, yet intense, complex of storms produced a long-track EF-1 tornado from Illinois into Gibson and Knox Counties in Indiana, as well as isolated, locally intense, damaging winds that were mainly in southeastern central Indiana.
episodes.167707: A cluster of thunderstorms developed along a leading edge of higher instability during the afternoon of Wednesday, May 18th. These storms moved from east central Minnesota, and northwest Wisconsin, southeastward toward west central Wisconsin and produced isolated large hail around Rice Lake. The largest hailstone was 1.25 inches in diameter.
episodes.167708: A significant hail event occurred during the daytime hours of May 19th, 2022 across Southeast-Central Minnesota and Western Wisconsin. A multicellular convective mode advanced in two waves with the first wave occurring through the morning hours in Southern MN, while the second wave produced a long-track supercell over the Twin Cities metro and Central Wisconsin. Both waves produced significant hail and damaging wind gusts. The synoptic setup included weak ridging and zonal flow in the Upper Midwest giving way to a deepening trough in the Pacific Northwest. A cold front was advancing eastward through the Dakotas. Over Iowa, a northward advancing warm front coupled with steep lapse rates in the mid levels (7.5-8��C/km) were able to drive development initially at the MN/IA border and eventually farther north into the Metro, then eastward. Upper-air soundings depicted a marginal environment for Supercell development with 50-60kt 0-6km shear and an elevated area of 1200 J/kg MUCAPE in the mid-levels. The SPC issued threat level for the day was slight to enhanced risk with most attention given to a significant hail potential. ||The storms that developed in the mid-late afternoon produced countless hailstones across the Twin Cities metro area, and into west central Wisconsin by the late afternoon. Beyond the typical 1 inch diameter hailstones, there were several hailstones up to 2 inches in diameter that fell over Washington County. A few other large hailstones fell over Le Sueur, Dakota and Goodhue Counties of southern Minnesota.
episodes.167709: A significant event occurred during the daytime hours of May 19th, 2022 across Eastern Minnesota and Western Wisconsin. A wave of storms in the afternoon produced a long-track supercell with large hail and damaging wind over the Twin Cities metro and West Central Wisconsin. The synoptic setup included weak ridging and zonal flow in the Upper Midwest giving way to a deepening trough in the Pacific Northwest. A cold front was advancing eastward through the Dakotas. Over Iowa, a northward advancing warm front coupled with steep lapse rates in the mid levels (7.5-8��C/km) were able to drive development initially at the MN/IA border and eventually farther north into the Metro, then eastward. Upper-air soundings depicted a marginal environment for Supercell development with 50-60kt 0-6km shear and an elevated area of 1200 J/kg MUCAPE in the mid-levels. The SPC issued threat level for the day was slight to enhanced risk with most attention given to a significant hail potential. ||The storms that developed in the mid-late afternoon over the Twin Cities metro area, moved into west central Wisconsin by the late afternoon and early evening. Several of the hailstones measured up to 2 inches in diameter and damaging winds occurred near Spring Valley and Elmwood.
episodes.167774: A strong Low Pressure system dropped south out of Canada.  This would produce convective showers and a few thunderstorms over the region, some of which would produce strong downdraft winds.
episodes.167853: An upper level shortwave trough combined with instability allowed convection to develop in the afternoon. One traffic fatality on Interstate 5 near Kelso, Washington is attributed to hail accumulating on highway.
episodes.167882: A surface low was situated over Iowa/Illinois/Missouri during the day of the 18th, with a  warm front extended eastward and across and just north of the Bluegrass State. SPC had placed much of our area in a marginal risk of severe weather early in the day, before upgrading to a slight category during a morning update. A secondary low also developed and moved into the state for the afternoon, creating a secondary warm front boundary - along which lift and all modes of severe weather were possible, with the best chances for wind and hail. There was enough low level sheer that an isolated tornado couldn't be ruled out. As a shortwave trough also approached eastern KY throughout the day, along with an MCS to our west, the atmosphere was primed for severe weather to occur across the southeastern portions of the CWA.
episodes.167922: Showers and thunderstorms developed along a frontal boundary stalled near southwest Virginia during the afternoon and evening of May 19th. Several storms became severe, which produced up to ping pong ball sized hail and damaging winds. Multiple trees were blown down around southwest Virginia as well as utility poles, which led to numerous power outages.
episodes.167985: Showers and thunderstorms developed during the evening hours along a warm front lifting north across the Ohio Valley.
episodes.167986: Showers and thunderstorms developed during the evening hours along a warm front lifting north across the Ohio Valley.
episodes.168019: Numerous showers and storms fired during the afternoon and evening of the 19th in the vicinity of a wavering frontal boundary over eastern Kentucky.  High amounts of instability and ample shear favored splitting supercells. While there were many reports of dime to quarter-sized hail, two particularly intense storms produced up to egg-size hail near Jackson and Stanton.
episodes.168111: Several rounds of  thunderstorms brought large hail and some damaging wind gusts to portions of northeast Tennessee, starting in the late evening hours of May 18 and continuing through the afternoon of May 19. Most of the reports were of large hail, with the largest being the size of a hen egg.
episodes.168112: Thunderstorms brought large hail to parts of southwest Virginia during the afternoon of May 19, with the largest reported hail being the size of a ping pong ball.
episodes.168199: An organized complex of thunderstorms accompanied a pronounced mesoscale convective vortex (MCV) as it tracked across Missouri and Illinois. A corridor of moderate to strong instability formed ahead of the MCV from southern Missouri into southern Illinois and Indiana. The storms moved northeast from southeast Missouri across southwest Illinois in the form of a squall line early in the evening, with locally damaging winds. After weakening for a couple hours, the storms then redeveloped over the Wabash Valley region into an organized cluster with an embedded supercell. The supercell produced a tornado that tracked into southwest Indiana.
episodes.168200: Two rounds of severe thunderstorms occurred. The first round during the mid afternoon hours was associated with a surge of higher dew points northward. Storms erupted along this effective front over southwest Indiana, which was beneath a region of warm moist wind flow at 850 mb. Very large hail accompanied a few of these storms. The second round was an organized complex of thunderstorms that accompanied a pronounced mesoscale convective vortex (MCV) that tracked across Missouri and Illinois. A corridor of moderate to strong instability formed ahead of the MCV from southern Missouri into southern Illinois and Indiana. After a brief lull over Illinois, the storms redeveloped during the evening over the Wabash Valley region as a small cluster with an embedded supercell. The supercell produced a tornado that tracked into southwest Indiana.
episodes.168201: An isolated severe thunderstorm occurred during the mid afternoon hours, associated with a surge of higher dew points northward. The storm erupted along this effective front over northwest Kentucky, which was beneath a region of warm moist wind flow at 850 mb. Large hail accompanied this storm.
episodes.168202: An organized complex of thunderstorms accompanied a pronounced mesoscale convective vortex (MCV) as it tracked across Missouri and Illinois. A corridor of moderate to strong instability formed ahead of the MCV from southern Missouri into southern Illinois and Indiana. The storms moved northeast across portions of southeast Missouri in the form of a squall line early in the evening, with isolated damaging winds.
episodes.168483: A potent mid level shortwave combined with weak instability and strong shear to generate strong to severe storms across central and north-central Wisconsin during the evening hours on Wednesday (5/18).  The strongest storms produced wind damage and half dollar size hail.
episodes.168488: Thunderstorms developed north of a stalled out warm front across western Wisconsin and tracked east through central Wisconsin during the early evening hours on Thursday (5/19).  The strongest storms produced isolated wind damage and hail up to quarter size.
episodes.168672: Increasing southeasterly lower tropospheric winds produced several leeward cloud streets extending from the Lower Florida Keys in the nearshore Gulf of Mexico waters.  Several waterspouts resulted.
episodes.168794: A weakening warm front lifting north into southern Virginia triggered scattered thunderstorms. A few of these storms produced hail up to the size of nickels in Pittsylvania and Montgomery counties.
episodes.169085: A complex of storms over southwestern Missouri during the early morning hours of May 19th, moved east northeast along the I-70 corridor. Some of the storms became severe with several reports of damaging winds.
episodes.169087: A complex of storms over southwestern Missouri during the early morning hours of May 19th, moved east northeast along the I-70 corridor. Some of the storms became severe with several reports of damaging winds.
episodes.169089: During the early afternoon of Thursday, May 19, 2022, a complex of thunderstorms expanded and intensified over sections of south-central Missouri. Thunderstorms quickly became strong to severe as the complex tracked east-northeast, impacting east-central Missouri, southeast Missouri, west-central Illinois and southwest Illinois. Numerous thunderstorms embedded within the broad complex exhibited signs of rotation, resulting in nine confirmed tornadoes. Of the nine tornadoes, six tornadoes occurred in Missouri and three occurred in Illinois. In Missouri, five of the six tornadoes were rated EF-0 and one tornado was rated EF-1. In Illinois, two tornadoes were rated EF-0, while the third was rated EF-1. In addition to the nine tornadoes, several locations were impacted by straight-line wind damage. The greatest impact from straight-line winds extended west to east through sections of southeast Missouri into southwest Illinois. The most extensive straight-line wind damage was in a swath from Desloge, MO through Chester, IL. Between the tornadoes and straight-line winds, much of the damage was similar in nature, taking out several trees, damaging outbuildings, machine sheds, and a few grain silos. Some residential homes also suffered damage, largely due to fallen trees, large limbs and/or flying debris. No fatalities nor injuries were reported.
episodes.169090: During the early afternoon of Thursday, May 19, 2022, a complex of thunderstorms expanded and intensified over sections of south-central Missouri. Thunderstorms quickly became strong to severe as the complex tracked east-northeast, impacting east-central Missouri, southeast Missouri, west-central Illinois and southwest Illinois. Numerous thunderstorms embedded within the broad complex exhibited signs of rotation, resulting in nine confirmed tornadoes. In Illinois, two tornadoes were rated EF-0, while the third was rated EF-1. In addition to the nine tornadoes, several locations were impacted by straight-line wind damage. The greatest impact from straight-line winds extended west to east through sections of southeast Missouri into southwest Illinois. The most extensive straight-line wind damage was in a swath from Desloge, MO through Chester, IL. Between the tornadoes and straight-line winds, much of the damage was similar in nature, taking out several trees, damaging outbuildings, machine sheds, and a few grain silos. Some residential homes also suffered damage, largely due to fallen trees, large limbs and/or flying debris. No fatalities nor injuries were reported.
episodes.169240: A west to east warm front slid north across central Kentucky into southern Indiana between May 19th and 20th. This caused scattered convection to breakout across the region. Scattered tree damage and power outages resulted across multiple southern Indiana counties.
episodes.169272: A warm front across Nebraska and northern Iowa served as the focus for midday convection, with a  few hail reports occurring in far northern Iowa. The associated surface low then moved into Iowa late in the day, resulting in additional isolated thunderstorms. One storm in west central Iowa produced a severe gust of 63 mph.
episodes.169332: On May 18th, strong daytime heating allowed for scattered thunderstorms to develop within Northwestern Kansas. Some of these thunderstorms yielded wind gusts up to 62 mph as well a hail up to a penny in size.
episodes.169517: Isolated severe thunderstorms developed late in the day across the far southeast plains, with wind gusts around 60 mph and hail around an inch observed.
episodes.169616: Isolated strong storms produced penny sized hail.
episodes.169623: A mesoscale convective complex moved southeastward across the region during the morning of the 18th. The complex weakened during the late morning with the loss of the low level jet and left an outflow boundary that focused storm development later that afternoon near the Arkansas border. Hail to golf balls in size and damaging winds were produced by the strongest storms.
episodes.169624: A nocturnal storm complex developed over southwest Kansas and northwest Oklahoma during the evening of the 18th moved eastward and reached the western edge of the Ozarks during the early morning of the 19th. The storm complex developed into a mesoscale convective vorticity center (MCV) and tracked northeastward across the region through the late morning and afternoon. The airmass on the eastern side of the MCV was unstable enough for severe storms to develop during the afternoon. The storms produced two EF-1 tornadoes in Phelps County south of I-44 near the towns of Beulah and Lecoma. Localized flash flooding was also observed near I-44 between Marshfield and Rolla. The storms also produce areas of widespread wind damage and localized flooding.
episodes.169660: A broken line of storms moved across most of western Wisconsin during the evening of May 18th. Some of these storms were strong enough to produce hail across parts of Taylor County. The largest reported hail was half dollar sized near Gilman (Taylor County).
episodes.169674: A line of storms moved into northern Oklahoma late on the 18th and early on the 19th, with numerous severe wind gusts reported. Isolated gusts up to 80 mph were recorded in portions of northwest Oklahoma.
episodes.169709: An easterly moving upper disturbance, combined with moderate levels of wind shear and moderate to high instability led to the development of severe thunderstorms which moved southeast across the area.  The majority of the severe storms impacted the northeast Panhandles however an isolated severe storm also crossed the southwest Texas Panhandle. These storms mostly produced some strong and damaging winds across the Oklahoma Panhandle, however in the Texas Panhandle large hail up to the size of baseballs was also reported.
episodes.169710: An easterly moving upper disturbance, combined with moderate levels of wind shear and moderate to high instability led to the development of severe thunderstorms which moved southeast across the area.  The majority of the severe storms impacted the northeast Panhandles however an isolated severe storm also crossed the southwest Texas Panhandle. These storms mostly produced some strong and damaging winds across the Oklahoma Panhandle, however in the Texas Panhandle large hail up to the size of baseballs was also reported with a lone supercell across the southwest Texas Panhandle.
episodes.169794: Strong to severe thunderstorms formed ahead of a mid-level shortwave and surface disturbance which moved through the Ohio Valley during the afternoon and evening hours on May 18th. Storms initially formed as part of an MCS which moved across southern Indiana and into central Kentucky. After the initial MCS dissipated, scattered cells formed along the southern flank of the antecedent MCS, causing wind damage and hail across central Kentucky.
episodes.169870: Two rounds of storms moved across southeast Minnesota on May 19th. The first occurred from late morning through the middle of the afternoon and produced primarily large hail across Mower and Olmsted Counties. The largest reported hail with this activity was ping pong ball sized near Lyle (Mower County), Adams (Mower County), south of Rochester (Olmsted County) and east of Rochester. The second round of storms also produced hail, although not as large as the earlier storms. The largest reported hail in the late afternoon was quarter sized north of Genoa (Olmsted County). A large tree, estimated to be four feet in diameter, was blown down near Whalan (Fillmore County). Flash flooding across eastern Winona County caused several mud slides, washouts and some cars were submerged in water. Winona County declared a state of emergency and the Governor of Minnesota authorized emergency assistance to help with the recovery.
episodes.169973: Isolated thunderstorms moved into western North Carolina during the morning. One of the storms produced up to nickel size hail in the Asheville area.
episodes.169974: Isolated to widely scattered thunderstorms moved over western North Carolina throughout the afternoon and evening. A few of the storms produced hail and brief damaging wind gusts.
episodes.170059: An area of low pressure tracking along a nearly stationary frontal boundary extending from the Ozarks into the Ohio River Valley brought several clusters of strong to severe thunderstorms to southeast Illinois during the afternoon and evening of May 19th.  One storm dropped quarter-sized hail west of Hardinville in Crawford County, while other cells produced wind gusts of around 60mph and minor wind damage across portions of Effingham and Lawrence Counties.
episodes.170090: A stationary front lingered across central Kentucky during the day on May 19th, with a warm and moist environment located along and south of this boundary. During the afternoon and evening hours, a negatively-tilted mid-level shortwave passed just north and west of the region, helping to add dynamic support to an already thermodynamically unstable environment. Storms formed near the front in the early afternoon as multicell clusters, with a few supercells moving along the southern flank of the convective activity. The strongest cells produced considerable amounts of large hail across central Kentucky, with hail sizes larger than baseballs being observed in Fayette and Harrison County.
episodes.170139: A lightning strike from an isolated thunderstorm struck a tree, destroying it.
episodes.170328: A wind event occurred mid to late evening across western portions of the CWA with radiational cooling after sunset. Being in the baroclinic zone of the storm system, high based convection occurred allowing for strong outflows with ample DCAPE values over 1200 J/kg. 60-70 mph was the frequent reports with only small hail occurring.

A brief and weak tornado touched down in St. Louis County near the city of Frontenac and moved north for just over a mile. The touchdown occurred 0.4 miles southwest of Frontenac and the tornado lifted 1 mile north of Frontenac. Damage caused by the tornado mainly consisted of downed trees and snapped limbs. Overall, the tornado was rated EF0 with a path length of 1.32 miles and a max path width of 50 yards. No deaths or injuries were reported.

A brief tornado with estimated maximum wind speeds of 80 mph impacted portions of central St. Louis County. The tornado developed around 5:06 p.m. 1.7 miles NW of the center of Creve Coeur, near the intersection of Kram Road and Olive Boulevard. The tornado ran nearly parallel to Timber Run Drive before turning northwest at Markaire Drive and impacted areas just southwest of North High School. The tornado crossed Fee Fee Road as it moved northwest and lifted over Seven Pines Drive at approximately 5:07 p.m. Several trees were damaged, power poles were snapped and a few homes were damaged due to falling limbs. Overall, the tornado was rated EF0 with a path length of 0.79 miles and a max path width of 50 yards. No deaths or injuries were reported.

Thunderstorm winds blew down several trees onto Illinois Route 155 in Ruma. Numerous tree limbs were blown down in Baldwin. In the Sparta and Eden areas, numerous trees, tree limbs and power lines were blown down. Several buildings in Sparta sustained minor damage from fallen trees and tree limbs.

Widespread wind damage across Chester. Numerous trees, tree limbs, power poles and power lines were blown down around town. Also, a couple of houses sustained damage from fallen trees.  Several businesses were damaged as well.

A weak tornado touched down over a residence just east of Summerfield Street/St. Jacob Road, 1 mile north of Summerfield, IL. Trees suffered damage on the property before the tornado continued north-northeast through a small, open field. The tornado impacted a row of trees on the north edge of the field, entered another field and lifted approximately one minute after initially developing. Overall, the tornado was rated EF0 with a path length of 0.23 miles and a max path width of 50 yards. No deaths or injuries were reported.
Thunderstorm winds blew off part of the roof of a house into a tree approximately 100 yards away.

A wind gust to 73 mph was measured in Cutler. A tree was reported down across a road a few miles southwest of Swanwick.

A weak tornado touched down briefly 2.8 miles east-southeast of Okawville, Illinois, traveled 1.6 miles northeast and lifted 3.9 miles east-northeast of Okawville, Illinois. A few sheds and outbuildings suffered damage along the path of the tornado, including one shed that was completely destroyed. Maximum wind speed of the tornado was estimated at 85 mph at the site of the destroyed shed. Crop damage was also observed. Overall, the tornado was rated EF0 with a path length of 1.65 miles and a max path width of 50 yards. No deaths or injuries were reported.
Thunderstorm winds uprooted a large tree in Addieville. In Nashville, numerous tree limbs were blown down around town, as well as several power lines. Also, a small shed was destroyed.
Thunderstorm winds blew down several trees, numerous tree limbs and several power lines.

A tornado with estimated maximum wind speeds of 110 mph impacted northern Clinton and southern Bond counties in Illinois. The tornado touched down around 5:57 PM 3.6 miles north of Breese (Clinton County), just west of Jamestown Road, about half a mile south of intersection with Tin Shanty Road. Three farms in this area sustained damage to a number of buildings, as well as one residence. The tornado continued to travel to the north northeast with additional damage to several more residences and outbuildings before crossing into southern Bond County, at the intersection of Keysport Road and Schrage Road. The tornado was rated EF1 in Clinton County with a path length of 5.75 miles and a max path width of 250 yards. No deaths or injuries were reported.
Thunderstorm winds blew off some shingles from the roof of a house as well as several tree limbs.

The tornado crossed into southern Bond County at the intersection of Keysport Road and Schrage Road. It continued to travel to the north northeast. It caused roof damage to an outbuilding as well as snapping off a couple of large trees at a farm on Drake School Road, just west of intersection with Millersburg Road. It eventually crossed Interstate 70 just southwest of Exit 45 on the southeast side of Greenville. It lifted and dissipated along Illinois Route 127 just north of intersection with Bowman Industrial Drive. The tornado was rated EF1 in Bond County with a path length of 10.9 miles and a max path width of 250 yards. No deaths or injuries were reported. Overall, the tornado was rated EF1 with a path length of 16.65 miles and a max path width of 250 yards.
